title: A Standard Contract Form Is a Risk Allocation You Can Read in Advance
summary: Standard construction contract forms from the AIA, ConsensusDocs and FIDIC families exist so that owners and contractors start from a known allocation of risk. This lesson explains the three families and the four mechanisms that decide most disputes: order of precedence, notices, conditions precedent and time bars.
body:
A standard contract form is not paperwork to sign. It is a pre-agreed answer to who carries which risk, and four small mechanisms inside it, precedence, notices, conditions precedent and time bars, decide more disputes than any large clause.

Recall

Q. What are the four tests in the Phase 8 checkpoint recording?

A. Accuracy, structure, composure and the hard question, each scored from 1 to 5.

Q. What are the three internal ways a partnership fails?

A. Governance capture, related-party dealing and handshake deals.

Q. What does a capital call clause need to say?

A. When a call can be made, how much notice is given, what happens if a partner does not fund, such as dilution or a priority loan, and any penalty multiplier.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Phase 9 is contracts, insurance, risk and audit. It begins here, because the construction contract is where most of a project's risk is allocated, and most developers sign it without reading the parts that will matter. Marco, your owner's project manager, joins me this week, because he lives with these clauses on site long after the lawyers have gone home.

The three families, in plain English

A standard form is a contract written by an industry body, used again and again, so that both sides already know what most clauses mean. Courts and arbitrators have interpreted many of them, which makes outcomes more predictable. You then amend the parts that do not fit your project.

AIA documents come from the American Institute of Architects. A typical set pairs an owner-contractor agreement, which holds the price and key commercial terms, with a separate document of general conditions, which holds the machinery: changes, claims, payment, termination. They are common in American building work and are generally seen as drafted from a design professional's perspective.

ConsensusDocs are a family of American forms produced by a coalition of industry associations, including owners, contractors and subcontractors, with the stated aim of a balanced allocation of risk.

FIDIC forms come from the International Federation of Consulting Engineers and are widely used on international projects. The Red Book is for construction where the employer designs, the Yellow Book for plant and design-build where the contractor designs, and the Silver Book for engineer-procure-construct turnkey work where the contractor takes most risk. Verify the current editions and their exact terms before relying on any of this [unverified — confirm independently].

Applied example. For a small apartment building with a design you own, the owner-design families, an AIA owner-contractor pair or the FIDIC Red Book abroad, are natural starting points. If you want one contractor to design and build, look at the design-build forms in each family instead. The choice of family follows the delivery method you chose in Week 52, not the other way round.

Mechanism one: order of precedence

In plain English: when two contract documents disagree, which one wins?

An order of precedence clause ranks the documents, for example: the agreement, then the special conditions, then the general conditions, then the specifications, then the drawings. Without one, a conflict between a drawing and a specification becomes an argument. With a bad one, the wrong document wins. Applied example, hypothetical: the specification calls for a heavier window assembly; the drawings show a lighter one; the price difference is 150,000 dollars. If specifications rank above drawings, the heavier window is included in the price. If not, the contractor may claim a change. Read the precedence clause against your own documents before you sign.

Mechanism two: notices

In plain English: a notice clause says how, when and to whom formal messages must be sent. Many contracts require written notice to a named person at a named address, by named methods, and say when a notice is treated as received. An email to the wrong person, or a comment in a site meeting, may not count. Notices are how claims, delays, changes and defaults become real.

Say that out loud now.

Mechanism three: conditions precedent

A condition precedent is something that must happen before a right exists. In a construction contract, a common example is that the contractor is entitled to extra time or money only if it gives notice within a stated period. The wording matters: "shall give notice" may be a mere obligation, while "shall not be entitled unless notice is given" is more likely to be read as a condition. Courts in different systems treat these words differently. Verify against the governing law.

Mechanism four: time bars

A time bar is a condition precedent with a clock: if notice is not given within, say, a fixed number of days of becoming aware of the event, the claim is lost. International forms are often read as containing strict time bars for claims, and American forms contain notice periods as well, though the periods and their effect differ by form, edition and amendment [unverified — confirm independently]. Owners like time bars because they force early warning. Contractors fear them because a valid claim can vanish on a technicality.

Marco's view from site

Marco's experience is that the four mechanisms fail in the same way: not through bad faith, but through ordinary busyness. A superintendent mentions ground water in a weekly meeting, everyone nods, the minute records "water noted", and nobody sends a notice. Six weeks later the dewatering bill arrives and the contractor discovers the claim window has closed. Or the owner's architect issues a sketch that changes a detail, the contractor builds it, and nobody records it as a change because it arrived by email.

His fix is a habit, not a clause. At the end of every site meeting, ask one question aloud: "Does anything we discussed today need a formal notice or a change order?" Write the answer in the minute, even if it is "no". Then the person responsible sends the notice that day, by the method the contract names. It takes two minutes a week. It turns the contract from a document in a drawer into the way the job is actually run, and it protects both sides from losing a right they did not know was ticking.

How the best do it

Experienced owners keep one set of standard amendments, sometimes called supplementary conditions, which they apply to a chosen form on every project, rather than rewriting the form each time. They also run a notices register on every job: every notice sent and received, the clause it relies on, the date and the deadline for a response. A small developer can copy both: one carefully negotiated amendment set, reviewed by counsel once and reused, and a simple register kept by the project manager.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: how a contract splits supply and services can affect indirect tax; confirm with an adviser. Liability: the form decides who carries design, ground and delay risk. Banking: lenders review the construction contract and usually want collateral assignment rights over it. Governance: decide who in your company may issue and receive notices. Estate: key contracts should survive a change in your circumstances through proper entity and signing authority. Exit: a buyer will read your claims history and open notices.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is signing a form whose machinery you have not read, then missing a notice or a deadline that the form treats as decisive. The control is a notices register and a one-page summary of every deadline in the contract, kept by your project manager from day one.

The beginner's mistake

Negotiating hard on price and ignoring the general conditions. The price is fixed once. The general conditions decide every change and claim afterwards.

Callback

In Week 52 Marco taught delivery methods and the FIDIC Red, Yellow and Silver books as procurement choices. This week turns the same books into operating manuals: once the method is chosen, the form's precedence, notice and time-bar clauses decide how the project is actually run.

Recap

Standard forms from AIA, ConsensusDocs and FIDIC pre-allocate risk and come with known interpretations. Four mechanisms decide most disputes: the order of precedence, notices, conditions precedent and time bars. Read them, amend them once, and keep a notices register.

Next: Ford, Failure forensics, on Failure Forensics: the Hyatt Regency walkway collapse and a change that travelled through a shop drawing.
checklist: I choose the contract family that matches my delivery method.
I read the order of precedence clause against my own drawings and specifications.
I know exactly how, to whom and by what method notices must be sent.
I know which notice obligations are conditions precedent.
I list every time bar in the contract with its period.
I keep one counsel-reviewed set of amendments and reuse it.
My project manager keeps a notices register from day one.
I decide in writing who may issue and receive notices for my company.
head: Field checklist
speak: A standard construction contract form is a pre-agreed allocation of risk. AIA forms come from the American Institute of Architects, ConsensusDocs from a coalition of American industry groups, and FIDIC from the International Federation of Consulting Engineers, with the Red Book where the employer designs, the Yellow Book for design-build, and the Silver Book for turnkey work. Choose the family that fits your delivery method. Then read four mechanisms. The order of precedence decides which document wins when two disagree. Notice clauses say how, when and to whom formal messages must go; a remark in a site meeting may not count. A condition precedent is something that must happen before a right exists. A time bar is a condition precedent with a clock: miss the notice period and the claim may be lost. Keep one reviewed set of amendments and a notices register from day one. Verify every form and period against the current edition.
terms: Order of precedence — a clause ranking contract documents so that, if they conflict, the higher-ranked one governs.
Condition precedent — something that must happen before a contractual right or obligation exists.
Time bar — a condition precedent with a deadline, after which a claim is lost if notice was not given.

hostile.q: Your amended contract adds strict time bars on every claim. Why should we bid on that?
hostile.a: Because the same clauses protect you as much as us, if we run them properly. Every time bar comes with a notices register we share with you, a named recipient and an agreed email address that counts as valid notice, and a monthly meeting where open notices are reviewed. The aim is early warning, not technical defeat. If any period is unworkable for a particular risk, tell us now and we will discuss it before you price it.

title: Hyatt Regency 1981: A Design Change That Travelled Through a Shop Drawing
summary: On 17 July 1981 two suspended walkways in the atrium of the Hyatt Regency hotel in Kansas City collapsed, killing 114 people. The connection that failed had been changed during the shop drawing process. This lesson takes the case through seven steps and draws a rule about how changes must move through a contract.
body:
The Hyatt Regency walkways fell because a change to a critical connection moved through the shop drawing process as if it were a detail, and nobody in the contract chain checked it as the design change it was.

Recall

Q. What does an order of precedence clause do?

A. It ranks the contract documents so that, when two disagree, the higher-ranked document governs.

Q. What is Rule 75?

A. Never let anyone sit on both sides of a transaction with an entity they owe a duty to unless the relationship is disclosed in writing, the price is benchmarked independently, and a party with no interest approves it first.

Q. What is a drag-along right?

A. A right for majority partners to require minority partners to join a sale of the whole venture on the same terms.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is a contracts week, and the Hyatt Regency is usually taught as an engineering failure. It was one. But it is also a lesson in contract administration: who is responsible for a change proposed by a fabricator, what a shop drawing review means, and what happens when everyone in the chain believes someone else checked. Every project you run will process hundreds of shop drawings. One of them will matter.

1. Timeline

The Hyatt Regency hotel in Kansas City, Missouri, opened in 1980 with a large atrium crossed by suspended walkways at the second, third and fourth floors. During construction, in 1979, part of the atrium roof collapsed; the incident prompted reviews, but the walkway connections were not identified as a problem. On the evening of 17 July 1981, during a crowded tea dance, the fourth-floor walkway and the second-floor walkway directly beneath it fell to the atrium floor. 114 people died and many more were injured. The investigation by the National Bureau of Standards traced the failure to the box-beam hanger rod connections at the fourth floor. Engineers responsible for the structural design later lost their licences in Missouri.

2. Key decisions

The original design hung both walkways from continuous rods running from the roof structure down through the fourth-floor walkway to the second-floor walkway. A continuous rod with a nut under each walkway is awkward to fabricate and install. During the shop drawing stage the steel fabricator proposed, and the change was approved, to replace each continuous rod with two rods: one from the roof to the fourth-floor walkway, and a second from the fourth-floor walkway down to the second. That one change meant the fourth-floor connection now carried the load of both walkways instead of one.

3. Assumptions

The fabricator assumed the engineer would check the change. The engineering firm's review stamp was applied on the assumption that the connection detail was a fabricator's matter or had been checked. Each party assumed the shop drawing review was a full design check by someone else. The investigation also found that even the original connection detail would not have met the capacity required by the building code, so the original design had been assumed adequate without being proved.

4. Incentives

The fabricator was paid to build efficiently, and the two-rod arrangement was easier. The design team was under schedule pressure to turn shop drawings around. Neither was paid to slow down and recalculate a connection that looked like a routine detail. Nobody's incentive pointed at the question "does this change the load path?"

Say that out loud now.

5. Warning signs ignored

The roof collapse in 1979 was a signal that the atrium structure deserved a fresh, critical review of every connection. Accounts given after the collapse suggested that some workers had found the walkways unsteady during construction and avoided them; treat that detail as reported rather than established. Above all, the change itself was a sign: any proposal that alters how a load travels to the ground is, by definition, a design change, whatever form it arrives in.

6. Point of no return

The point of no return was the approval of the shop drawing without a calculation. Once the doubled-load connection was fabricated and installed, nothing in the ordinary course of operation would reveal it until the walkways were heavily loaded, which happened on the night of the dance.

7. Root cause

The root cause was a change to the load path made through the shop drawing process without anyone treating it as a design change requiring the engineer of record's calculation. The contract chain allowed responsibility for the connection to fall into the gap between fabricator and engineer. Underneath that sat an original connection that had never been proved to code.

Marco's view: the contract lesson

A shop drawing is a document prepared by a contractor or fabricator showing exactly how it will make and install part of the work. Most contract forms say that the designer's review of a shop drawing is for general conformance with the design intent, and that it does not relieve the contractor of responsibility for its own work or approve a change unless the change is specifically identified and accepted [unverified — confirm independently]. That wording is protective, but it creates a dangerous gap if everyone reads it as meaning someone else is responsible. As owner, your control is a rule in the contract and on site: any proposed deviation from the design must be flagged on the submittal as a deviation, routed to the designer of record as a change request, and accepted only in writing with the supporting calculation for anything structural or life-safety related. Professional sign-off required: structural engineer of record.

This is the same discipline Week 49 taught for scope changes. A change is a change whether it arrives as a change order, a request for information, an email or a shop drawing. The route must be the same.

What a small developer copies

Write a four-line submittal procedure into your construction contract and your project manual. First, the contractor must mark every submittal "no deviation" or "deviation proposed", and describe any deviation in words. Second, a deviation is a change request, logged in the same register as change orders, with its own number. Third, structural, fire and life-safety deviations go to the relevant designer of record, who must accept or reject them in writing with the basis for the decision. Fourth, nothing marked as a deviation is fabricated until that written acceptance exists.

Then test it once on every project. Pick a structural submittal at random and ask your project manager to show you the deviation box, the register entry and the acceptance. If any of the three is missing, the procedure exists on paper only. This is a composite drill, but it takes ten minutes and it is the cheapest structural safety check an owner can make.

The prevention rule

Rule 77: Never let a change to the design reach the field through a shop drawing, submittal or email unless it is flagged as a change and the designer of record accepts it in writing, with the calculation for anything structural or life-safety.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a review process in which every party believes another party did the check. The control is a submittal procedure that requires deviations to be declared, a named reviewer for each discipline, and a written acceptance that states what was and was not checked.

The beginner's mistake

Treating shop drawings as administration to be turned around quickly. Most are. The one that changes a load path is the most important document on the project.

Callback

Rule 76, last week, said that nobody should hold the money, write the reports and choose the reviewer alone, because a check that no independent party performs is not a check. The Hyatt Regency is the same failure in steel: a review that each party assumed the other had done.

Recap

A fabricator's proposal to split continuous hanger rods doubled the load on the fourth-floor connection, the change was approved through shop drawing review without a calculation, and on 17 July 1981 the walkways fell. Rule 77 routes every design change through the designer of record in writing, whatever form it arrives in.

Next: Roman, Risk and the lender's view, on The Money: what notices, precedence and time bars are worth in dollars.
checklist: Every submittal must declare any deviation from the design.
Every declared deviation is routed to the designer of record as a change request.
Structural and life-safety changes need a written calculation before acceptance.
Each discipline has a named reviewer for shop drawings.
Written acceptances state what was and was not checked.
I treat a change arriving by email or sketch exactly like a change order.
After any structural incident during construction, I order a fresh review of related connections.
I never let schedule pressure set the turnaround time for a structural change review.
head: Field checklist
rule: Rule 77: Never let a change to the design reach the field through a shop drawing, submittal or email unless it is flagged as a change and the designer of record accepts it in writing, with the calculation for anything structural or life-safety.
speak: On 17 July 1981, during a tea dance at the Hyatt Regency hotel in Kansas City, the fourth-floor and second-floor walkways in the atrium collapsed. 114 people died. The original design hung both walkways from continuous rods. During shop drawings, the fabricator proposed replacing each continuous rod with two rods, one from the roof to the fourth floor and another from the fourth floor down to the second. The change was approved without a calculation, and it doubled the load on the fourth-floor connection. Investigators also found the original connection had not been proved to code. Each party assumed someone else had checked. The contract lesson is that a change is a change, however it arrives. Rule 77: no design change reaches the field through a shop drawing, submittal or email unless it is flagged as a change and the designer of record accepts it in writing, with the calculation for anything structural or life-safety.
terms: Shop drawing — a contractor's or fabricator's detailed drawing showing exactly how it will make and install part of the work.
Submittal — any document a contractor sends for the design team's review, such as shop drawings, product data or samples.
Load path — the route by which loads travel through a structure to the ground.

hostile.q: Your contractor proposed a cheaper connection detail and your architect stamped it. Who is responsible if it fails?
hostile.a: Responsibility depends on the contract and the law, which is exactly why our procedure does not rely on a stamp. Any deviation must be declared on the submittal, routed to the structural engineer of record as a change request, and accepted only in writing with a calculation. The acceptance says what was checked. If that record does not exist for a structural change, the change is not accepted and does not get built. I can show you the submittal log and the acceptance for every structural deviation on this job.

title: What Notices, Precedence and Time Bars Are Worth in Dollars
summary: The small mechanisms of a construction contract move real money: a missed notice can erase a claim, a strict time bar can raise every bid, and an unresolved conflict between documents becomes a change order. This lesson prices each one and shows how they reach your budget, your loan and your personal balance sheet.
body:
The clauses that look administrative carry money in both directions: a strict time bar can protect your budget from a claim, but contractors price that risk into every bid, and a poorly coordinated set of documents turns each conflict into a change order you pay for.

Recall

Q. What is Rule 77?

A. Never let a change to the design reach the field through a shop drawing, submittal or email unless it is flagged as a change and the designer of record accepts it in writing, with the calculation for anything structural or life-safety.

Q. In the handshake example, why did fighting have a negative expected value for both partners?

A. Because the probability-weighted gain was smaller than the legal costs plus each partner's share of the extra interest during a frozen sale.

Q. What is penalty dilution?

A. Crediting a partner who funds another's missed capital call with more than it paid, which reduces the defaulting partner's share by more than straight dilution would.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a lender reads your construction contract to answer one question: how likely is the budget to hold? Every mechanism we met on Day 1 changes that answer. You need to be able to say, in dollars, what you gave up or gained by choosing a form and amending it.

Worked example one: the claim that a time bar removes

All figures hypothetical. Midway through a 20,000,000 dollar building, the contractor meets rock that the ground report did not predict. Extra excavation costs 400,000 dollars and adds 30 days. Suppose your contract allocates unforeseen ground to you as owner, but only if the contractor gives notice within a fixed period of becoming aware of it. The contractor's superintendent mentions the rock in a meeting but sends no written notice until well after the period has passed.

Step 1. If the time bar is enforced strictly, the contractor bears the 400,000 dollars and the time.

Step 2. If the time bar is not enforced, perhaps because the governing law treats it leniently, or because your own conduct waived it, you pay 400,000 dollars plus the contractor's time-related costs for 30 days. Say those run 8,000 dollars a day for site overhead and equipment: 240,000 dollars. Total 640,000 dollars.

Step 3. Your own cost of 30 days of delay: if 15,000,000 dollars of the loan is drawn at 7 percent, interest is about 15,000,000 times 0.07 divided by 365, roughly 2,900 dollars a day, or about 86,000 dollars for 30 days.

So whether a single notice clause holds can swing your outcome by more than 700,000 dollars on one event. That is the number a lender is really asking about.

Worked example two: what strict time bars cost in the bid

Contractors are not naive. When they read a contract with strict, short time bars and wide owner protections, many add a risk premium to their price or a larger contingency. Suppose bidders add 1.5 percent to a 20,000,000 dollar price for that reason. That is 300,000 dollars, paid on every project whether or not a single claim arises.

Step 1. Expected claim value you avoid: suppose, over many similar projects, you would face on average one valid but late-notified claim of about 400,000 dollars every two projects. Expected saving per project: 200,000 dollars.

Step 2. Premium you pay per project: 300,000 dollars.

Step 3. Net: you pay 100,000 dollars a project for strictness you could get more cheaply through a fair notice period and a well-run notices register that gives you early warning anyway.

Say that out loud now.

The percentages and frequencies here are hypothetical; real premiums vary by market and contractor appetite, and are commercial practice, not a standard. The lesson holds: one-sided risk allocation is not free. Somebody prices it.

Worked example three: the price of an uncoordinated document set

Before bidding, your design team's documents contain conflicts between drawings and specifications. Suppose a coordination review by your project manager and designers finds ten conflicts with an average price consequence of 50,000 dollars each. Unresolved, with an order of precedence that does not favour you on each one, that is up to 500,000 dollars of potential change orders. The review costs 40,000 dollars. Even if half the conflicts would have gone your way, the review returns about 250,000 dollars of avoided exposure for 40,000 dollars. Precedence is the safety net. Coordination is the fix.

How this reaches the loan

A lender's monitor reading your contract will score its risk allocation. Unforeseen ground left with the owner, loose notice clauses and an uncoordinated set all increase the probability of overrun, and a lender may respond with a larger hard-cost contingency, a lower loan amount or a stronger cost-overrun guarantee. Each of those is real money: a contingency increase of 2 percent of 20,000,000 dollars is 400,000 dollars of capital that has to come from somewhere, usually equity. Negotiating the contract well is part of negotiating the loan.

Five questions the lender's monitor will ask about your contract

Prepare written answers before the monitor's first visit. They are the questions Roman would ask from the lender's chair.

  1. Which standard form did you use, which edition, and what did your amendments change?
  2. Who carries unforeseen ground, design development, escalation and delay, and is each allocation matched by a contingency line or a guarantee?
  3. What are the notice periods for claims and delays, and who on your side receives notices?
  4. Was a coordination review done before tender, and how many conflicts did it find and resolve?
  5. How many notices and claims are open today, and what is your realistic estimate of their value?

A borrower who answers these in writing, with the notices register attached, changes the monitor's first report from "risks to be assessed" to "risks identified and controlled". That sentence tends to travel up to the credit committee and back down as a smaller contingency demand or a lighter guarantee. In money terms, good contract administration is one of the few levers you hold that can reduce both your cost and your personal exposure at the same time.

Warrick's Wealth Ledger

Open notices and pending claims are contingent liabilities of the project, and if you have signed a cost-overrun or completion guarantee, they may become yours. Keep a one-line summary each month: the number of open claims, their total value as claimed, your realistic estimate, and how much of that would land on any guarantee you have given. Add it to the guarantee schedule from last week. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any personal financial decision.

The reverse is also true. A clean claims register, kept current, is an asset on your reputation's balance sheet: lenders and investors who see it on one project will offer better terms on the next.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is assuming the toughest contract is the cheapest. The control is to price your amendments both ways, the claims they prevent and the premium they add, before you issue the tender.

The beginner's mistake

Waiving a time bar by conduct without meaning to, for example by negotiating the merits of a late claim without reserving your rights, then finding the bar no longer protects you. Day 4 covers how that happens.

Callback

In Week 51 Quincy and Nadia built contingency structures and cost-to-complete forecasts. A notices register is the earliest input to that forecast: every notice is a possible future draw on contingency, visible months before the invoice arrives.

Recap

One notice clause can swing a single event by hundreds of thousands of dollars. Strict time bars save claims but are priced into bids. Coordination before tender is far cheaper than precedence after it. All of it reaches the loan, the contingency and any guarantee you sign.

Next: LEX, Contracts and law, on The Rules: how courts treat notices, conditions precedent and time bars.
checklist: I can price the swing on one claim if a time bar holds or fails.
I convert any delay into daily interest on the drawn loan balance.
I price each owner-favourable amendment against the bid premium it may add.
I commission a document coordination review before tender.
I know how my contract's risk allocation affects the lender's contingency demand.
I keep a monthly summary of open notices and claims.
I add claims exposure under my guarantees to my personal guarantee schedule.
I reserve my rights in writing before discussing the merits of any late claim.
head: Field checklist
speak: The clauses that look administrative move real money. Hypothetically, a contractor hits unforeseen rock costing 400,000 dollars and 30 days, but gives written notice late. If the time bar holds, the contractor carries it. If it fails, you pay 400,000 plus perhaps 240,000 of time-related costs, and your own loan interest on 15,000,000 drawn at 7 percent adds about 86,000. One clause swings the outcome by more than 700,000 dollars. But strictness is priced: if bidders add 1.5 percent to a 20,000,000 dollar contract for harsh time bars, that is 300,000 on every job, more than the claims it typically prevents. And a coordination review costing 40,000 before tender can avoid hundreds of thousands in precedence change orders. Lenders read all of this and adjust contingency and guarantees. Keep open claims on your personal guarantee schedule.
terms: Risk premium — the extra amount a bidder adds to its price to cover risks the contract places on it.
Coordination review — a check of drawings and specifications for conflicts before tender.
Time-related costs — a contractor's costs that grow with duration, such as site overhead, supervision and equipment.

hostile.q: Your contract leaves unforeseen ground with you as owner. Why should we lend against that?
hostile.a: Because we priced it rather than hid it. Our geotechnical investigation was extended to reduce the unknowns, the remaining ground risk is covered by a dedicated contingency line sized from our downside case, and the contract requires written notice within a fixed period so we see any claim early. Pushing the risk onto the contractor would have added a premium to every bid, which we estimated was more than the expected cost. Here is that comparison.

title: How Courts Treat Notices, Conditions Precedent and Time Bars
summary: Whether a missed notice really erases a claim depends on the wording of the clause, the governing law and the conduct of both parties. This lesson explains how courts approach notice provisions, conditions precedent and time bars, the doctrines that soften them, and how Canada and Guyana approach the point.
body:
A time bar works only if its words are clear, the notice machinery was followed, and neither party's conduct has undone it, so your protection lies in precise drafting, strict administration and never waiving a right by accident.

Recall

Q. On one unforeseen-ground event, how much could the time bar swing the owner's outcome in the Day 3 example?

A. More than 700,000 dollars, counting the claim, the contractor's time-related costs and the owner's own interest during delay.

Q. Why is "fair value" in a joint venture clause a defect?

A. Because it is a handshake term written down: it names no number, method or date, so each partner can hold a different version.

Q. What makes a deadlock clause workable?

A. Clear steps, from escalation to mediation to a final mechanism such as a buy-sell, with time limits, and a final step both partners could actually afford.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, you will be on both sides of these clauses. As owner you will want time bars to protect your budget, and as a party to other contracts, such as with your lender or a joint venture partner, you will need to meet notice requirements yourself. The law here rewards precision and punishes casualness. Everything that follows is concept. Verify it against the primary source and the governing law before you rely on it.

Notice provisions: strict and literal

In plain English: if a contract says how a notice must be given, do it exactly that way.

Courts in many common-law systems read notice clauses closely. If the clause requires written notice, delivered by hand, courier or a named email address, to a named person, an informal message to someone else may not count, however clear its content. Many clauses also contain deemed receipt rules, which treat a notice as received at a stated time after sending, for example the next business day after email. Those rules decide when a response period starts. The practical control is to treat every contractual notice as a formal document: the right form, the right recipient, the right method, and proof of delivery kept on file.

Two small habits prevent most notice failures. First, if the person or address named in the contract changes, give formal notice of the new details under the notice clause itself, because many clauses say notices to the old address remain valid until you do. Second, if the contract allows email, name a shared project address rather than one person's inbox, so a notice is never lost because someone was on leave or left the company.

Conditions precedent: clear words required

A condition precedent bars a right unless the condition is met. Because that outcome is severe, courts in many systems require clear words before treating a notice obligation as a condition. Wording such as "the contractor shall not be entitled to any extension of time or additional payment unless notice is given within the stated period" is more likely to be read as a condition precedent than "the contractor shall give notice promptly". If you want a time bar to bite, the drafting must say what is lost and when. If you are the party giving notice, assume every notice clause is a condition until your lawyer tells you otherwise.

What softens a time bar

Several doctrines can soften a strict time bar, and they vary by jurisdiction. Verify each against the primary source.

Waiver and estoppel. If an owner, knowing a notice was late, behaves as if it were valid, for example by negotiating the merits of the claim, paying part of it or granting time on it without reserving its position, a court may find the owner has given up the right to rely on the bar, or is prevented from relying on it because the contractor relied on that conduct.

The prevention principle. In some common-law systems, a party cannot benefit from a delay it caused. If the owner's own act delays the work and the contract has no mechanism to extend time for that act, the owner may be unable to enforce the completion date or deduct liquidated damages. Well-drafted forms avoid this by giving extensions for owner-caused delay.

Good faith. Some systems recognise duties of good faith or honest performance in contracts. In Canada, the Supreme Court of Canada in Bhasin v Hrynew, 2014, recognised a duty of honest contractual performance [unverified — confirm independently]. Such duties do not usually override clear terms, but they can affect how a party may exercise rights such as a time bar.

Say that out loud now.

Reserving your rights

The practical answer to waiver is a reservation of rights: a written statement that you are considering or responding to a matter without giving up any right under the contract, including the right to rely on a time bar. Applied example, hypothetical. A contractor submits a ground claim 40 days after the event, beyond a 28-day notice period in its contract. Your reply should acknowledge receipt, state that the notice appears to fall outside the contractual period, reserve all your rights including under that clause, and only then say whether you are willing to discuss the facts. Negotiations about settlement are often conducted on a without-prejudice basis, meaning they cannot later be used as evidence of an admission, but the protection and its limits vary by jurisdiction. Professional sign-off required: construction lawyer.

Two Systems

A conceptual comparison, to be verified against primary source before reliance. Canada's common-law provinces generally enforce clearly drafted notice and time-bar provisions, and Canadian courts have also recognised the duty of honest performance; Quebec applies its civil code, which includes good faith principles, to contracts. Guyana is a common-law jurisdiction whose courts have historically drawn on English case law, and whose final appellate court is the Caribbean Court of Justice; English authorities on conditions precedent, waiver and the prevention principle are likely to be persuasive there, though not binding. In both systems the governing-law and dispute-resolution clauses of the contract matter as much as the general law, and international projects often choose a neutral law and arbitration. Verify against the primary source and take advice from counsel admitted in each jurisdiction.

Applied example: drafting the clause you want

Hypothetical. You want early warning without an unfair trap. A balanced clause might say: notice of any event that may lead to a claim must be given in writing to the named owner's representative within a stated number of days of the contractor becoming aware of it; the notice need only describe the event and its likely effect, with details to follow; and if notice is not given in that time, the contractor is not entitled to additional time or money for the event. That is clear enough to work as a condition precedent, and fair enough that a contractor can comply. The period itself is commercial, not a standard.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is losing the protection of a time bar by your own conduct, especially by negotiating a late claim without a written reservation of rights. The control is a rule: no response to any late or doubtful claim leaves your office without a reservation, reviewed by your project manager or counsel.

The beginner's mistake

Assuming a time bar is self-executing. It is a right you must assert, in writing, at the right time, and it can be lost by silence or by friendliness.

Callback

In Week 20 LEX taught that remedies follow breach, and that what binds depends on wording and intention. Today is the same lesson in construction dress: whether a notice clause binds as a condition depends on its words, and whether it still binds depends on both parties' conduct.

Recap

Follow notice clauses literally. Draft conditions precedent with clear words saying what is lost. Know that waiver, estoppel, the prevention principle and good faith duties can soften a time bar, and reserve your rights in writing before discussing any late claim. Verify everything against the governing law.

Next: Petra, Scheduling, on The Numbers: counting the days to a notice deadline, step by step.
checklist: Every contractual notice I send uses the exact form, recipient and method required.
I keep proof of delivery for every notice sent and received.
I know the deemed receipt rule for each method of notice.
Clauses I want as time bars state what is lost and when.
I assume every notice clause is a condition precedent unless counsel says otherwise.
Every response to a late claim contains a written reservation of rights.
My contract grants extensions for owner-caused delay, to avoid the prevention principle.
I verify governing law and dispute resolution before relying on any time bar.
head: Field checklist
speak: A time bar works only if its words are clear, the notice machinery was followed, and neither party's conduct undid it. Courts in many systems read notice clauses literally: right form, right recipient, right method, with deemed receipt rules deciding when the clock starts. Because a condition precedent can wipe out a right, courts usually want clear words saying what is lost if notice is late. Several doctrines can soften a time bar: waiver and estoppel if you act as though a late notice were valid, the prevention principle if your own act caused the delay without an extension mechanism, and duties of good faith or honest performance in some systems. So never discuss a late claim without first reserving your rights in writing. Canada and Guyana both work from common-law foundations here, with Quebec applying its civil code. Verify everything against the primary source and the governing law.
terms: Waiver — giving up a contractual right, which can happen through conduct as well as words.
Prevention principle — the doctrine that a party should not benefit from a delay it caused.
Reservation of rights — a written statement that a party responds to a matter without giving up any right under the contract.

hostile.q: You negotiated our late ground claim for two months. How can you now say it is time-barred?
hostile.a: Because every letter we sent you, from the first acknowledgement, stated that your notice appeared to fall outside the contractual period and reserved all our rights under that clause, and our discussions were held on a without-prejudice basis. We have been willing to discuss the facts, and we still are. But we did not waive the notice requirement, and we said so in writing each time. If you believe the clause does not apply for another reason, put it to us in writing and we will take advice.

title: Counting the Days to a Notice Deadline
summary: A notice deadline is a calculation, not a feeling: which day counts as day zero, whether the period runs in calendar or working days, and when a notice is treated as received. This lesson works three deadline calculations step by step and then prices what a missed one costs.
body:
Most missed notice deadlines are not missed by weeks. They are missed by a day or two, because someone counted from the wrong day, used calendar days instead of working days, or forgot when a notice is treated as received.

Recall

Q. What can undo a time bar through the owner's own conduct?

A. Waiver or estoppel, for example negotiating the merits of a late claim without a written reservation of rights.

Q. In the related-party fee test, what four figures do you compute?

A. The fee charged, the benchmark fee, the excess, and who carries the excess, including the connected partner's net gain after its own equity share.

Q. What is a shotgun clause?

A. A buy-sell mechanism in which one partner names a price and the other must either buy at that price or sell at it.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a schedule is a chain of dates, and so is a contract's notice machinery. Your project manager will track hundreds of activities; the notice deadlines are the few that can cost or save six figures in a single day. You should be able to check any one of them yourself in two minutes.

The rules you need before you count

Every count needs three answers from the contract itself, and the answers differ between forms and amendments, so read them each time.

  1. What starts the clock? Often it is when a party became aware, or should have become aware, of the event, not when the event began.
  2. Calendar days or working days? A working day is usually defined to exclude weekends and stated public holidays; check the definition.
  3. How is the day of the trigger treated, and when is a notice received? Many contracts and many legal systems exclude the trigger day from the count; deemed receipt rules say when a notice sent by a given method counts as received.

For the examples below, assume the trigger day is excluded and is called Day 0. That is an assumption for teaching; verify it against your contract and the governing law.

Worked example one: a calendar-day period

Hypothetical. The contract requires notice of any claim event within 28 days of the contractor becoming aware of it. On a Wednesday, the contractor's site engineer sees water entering an excavation that the ground report did not predict. That Wednesday is Day 0.

Step 1. Count 28 calendar days. Day 7 is the next Wednesday, Day 14 the Wednesday after, Day 21 the third, and Day 28 the fourth Wednesday.

Step 2. The notice must be received by the end of Day 28, the fourth Wednesday after the event, unless the contract says the deadline moves when it falls on a non-working day. Here it is a Wednesday, so it does not move.

Step 3. Work back to an internal deadline. Your procedure should aim to send the notice within a week, by Day 7, leaving three weeks of margin for a holiday, a sick day or a lost email.

Worked example two: a working-day period with a holiday

Hypothetical. A different contract requires notice within 10 working days. The event is again noticed on a Wednesday, Day 0. The first Monday after it is a public holiday under the contract's definition.

Step 1. Count working days. Thursday is 1, Friday 2. The Monday is a holiday and does not count. Tuesday is 3, Wednesday 4, Thursday 5, Friday 6. The next Monday is 7, Tuesday 8, Wednesday 9, Thursday 10.

Step 2. The deadline is that Thursday, fifteen calendar days after the event. Without the holiday it would have been the Wednesday, fourteen days after.

Say that out loud now.

Step 3. Notice the trap. Someone who counted "two weeks" would choose the Wednesday and be safe here by luck. Someone who read "10 days" as calendar days would choose the Saturday ten days after the event and be early, which is harmless. Someone who started counting on the Wednesday itself, treating it as Day 1, would choose the Wednesday and still be safe. The danger runs the other way when a period is calendar days and someone assumes working days: they will be late. Always confirm which kind of day the clause means.

Worked example three: deemed receipt and the response clock

Hypothetical. The contract says notices may be sent by email to the named address, and an email sent after 5 pm, or on a non-working day, is treated as received at 9 am on the next working day. The owner must respond to a claim notice within 14 days of receipt.

Step 1. The contractor emails a claim notice at 6.15 pm on a Friday.

Step 2. Deemed receipt: 9 am on the following Monday.

Step 3. With Monday as Day 0 for the response clock, 14 calendar days later is the Monday two weeks on. The owner's response must be received by then.

Step 4. The lesson for both sides. The contractor gained nothing by sending late on Friday, and the owner lost nothing by not reading email over the weekend. But if the owner's team had counted from the Friday, they would believe their deadline was three days earlier than it is, and might rush a reply that should have carried a careful reservation of rights.

Worked example four: what one missed day costs

Hypothetical. In example one, the contractor sends the notice on Day 29, one day late. The event caused 30 days of delay and 400,000 dollars of extra direct cost. The contractor's time-related costs are 8,000 dollars a day, and the contract has liquidated damages, agreed damages for late completion, of 5,000 dollars a day.

Step 1. If the notice had been on time and the claim valid: the contractor recovers 400,000 dollars direct, plus 30 times 8,000, which is 240,000 dollars of time-related costs, and receives a 30-day extension, so it avoids 30 times 5,000, which is 150,000 dollars of liquidated damages. Total value to the contractor: 790,000 dollars.

Step 2. If the time bar holds: the contractor recovers none of it and may owe the liquidated damages. One day late cost about 790,000 dollars.

Step 3. From the owner's chair, that is the same amount you would rely on the clause for, which is why you must not waive it by conduct while it is in dispute. Rates and periods here are hypothetical; liquidated damages amounts are commercial terms, not standards.

Notice what the contractor's strongest argument would be in that case: not that the clause is unfair, but that the clock started later than the owner thinks. "Becoming aware" is a question of fact, which is why contemporaneous records, the site diary, photographs and meeting minutes, decide so many of these disputes. Vera's Week 82 on records will return to this. For now, the scheduling lesson is that the start date deserves as much evidence as the deadline.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is counting a deadline from memory instead of from the clause. The control is a notices register with a column for the trigger date, the clause, the type of days, the deemed receipt rule and the computed deadline, checked by a second person.

The beginner's mistake

Treating "28 days" and "four weeks" and "a month" as the same thing. They are not, and a month is not even the same length twice.

Callback

In Week 50 Petra taught critical path scheduling: logic, float and who owns it. A notice deadline is an activity with zero float. Put it in the schedule as one, with an internal milestone a week earlier.

Recap

Before counting, find the trigger, the type of day and the deemed receipt rule. Count from Day 0, check for holidays, and set an internal deadline a week early. One missed day can be worth hundreds of thousands of dollars to either side.

Next: Marco, Owner's project management, on The Room: the meeting where a contractor arrives with a stack of late claims.
checklist: I find what starts the clock before counting any notice period.
I confirm whether a period runs in calendar or working days.
I check the contract's definition of working day and its holidays.
I apply the deemed receipt rule for each method of notice.
I set an internal deadline at least a week before the contractual one.
My notices register shows trigger, clause, day type, receipt rule and deadline.
A second person checks every computed notice deadline.
I price what a missed deadline would cost each side.
head: Field checklist
speak: Notice deadlines are usually missed by a day or two, so count them properly. First find three things in the clause: what starts the clock, whether the period is calendar or working days, and when a notice is treated as received. Hypothetically, with 28 calendar days from a Wednesday, the deadline is the fourth Wednesday after. With 10 working days and a public holiday on the first Monday, the deadline moves to the second Thursday, fifteen calendar days later. An email sent at 6.15 on a Friday evening may be deemed received at 9 on Monday, so a 14-day response clock starts then. And one missed day can cost a contractor the direct cost, the time-related costs and relief from liquidated damages, in this example about 790,000 dollars. Keep a notices register with every deadline computed and checked by a second person, and set your own deadline a week early.
terms: Working day — a day counted for a contractual period, usually excluding weekends and defined holidays.
Deemed receipt — a contractual rule fixing when a notice counts as received, depending on how it was sent.
Liquidated damages — a sum agreed in advance as damages for a specified breach, such as late completion.

hostile.q: Your notice arrived on day 29. Why should we accept a claim the contract says is barred?
hostile.a: Because before you decide, I would ask you to check the count. The contract excludes the day of awareness, and our engineer became aware of the water's effect on the work on the Thursday, not the Wednesday, as his site diary and the photographs show. Counting from the Thursday as Day 0, the notice arrived on Day 28, within the period. If you count it differently, please set out your count in writing and we will review it with counsel.

title: The Meeting Where the Contractor Brings a Stack of Late Claims
summary: Months into a job, the contractor's project manager arrives with several claims, some of them notified late. This lesson scripts the owner's side of the meeting: how to keep the relationship working, how to protect your contractual position, and what never to say while doing both.
body:
When a contractor arrives with late claims, your job in the room is to keep the work moving and the relationship civil while protecting every contractual right you have, and that means listening fully, committing to nothing on the spot, and putting a reservation of rights in writing before any discussion of merits.

Recall

Q. In the working-day example, why did the deadline move from Wednesday to Thursday?

A. Because a public holiday under the contract's definition fell inside the period and did not count as a working day.

Q. In the related-party meeting, what three steps should you name?

A. Written disclosure of the interest, an independent benchmark, and a decision by the non-conflicted partner, with a date.

Q. What should a partner agreement say about death, disability and divorce?

A. Who may acquire the affected partner's interest, at what price and by what method, how the purchase is funded, and what rights the affected partner or estate keeps meanwhile.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the contractor is still building your project the day after this meeting. Win the argument and lose the relationship, and you will pay for it in slower work, defensive record keeping and every grey-area decision going against you. Keep the relationship and lose your contractual position, and you will pay for it in money. The skill is doing both.

The scene

This is a composite example. Five months into a hypothetical 20,000,000 dollar residential build, the contractor's project manager asks for a meeting. He brings four claims: a ground claim of 400,000 dollars, notified within time; a design-change claim of 180,000 dollars, notified well after the contract's notice period; a delay claim for 30 days caused, he says, by late approvals from your architect, notified late; and an escalation claim for steel of 120,000 dollars, which your contract allocates to the contractor. He is frustrated, the site is behind, and he says: "We need these settled this month or I'll have to slow down."

The question behind the question

On the surface he is asking for 700,000 dollars and 30 days. Underneath he may be telling you that his company is under cash pressure, that he is being pushed by his own management, or that he believes your side caused real problems. The threat to slow down is usually pressure, not a plan; a contractor that deliberately slows work may itself be in breach. Do not respond to the threat. Respond to the information.

The lines to say

Open by acknowledging. "Thank you for bringing these together. I can see the site is under pressure, and I want to work through them properly."

Separate the claims, out loud. "Let's take them one at a time, because they're in different places under the contract."

Signal the process. "For each one we'll review the notice, the facts and the clause, and we'll respond in writing by a date I'll give you today."

Protect the position without fighting it in the room. "On the two that came in after the notice period, our written response will reserve our rights under the contract. That doesn't mean we won't look at the facts. It means we're not giving anything up while we do."

Say that out loud now.

Address the cash pressure, if it is real, through the contract. "If valued work is outstanding, let's make sure it's in this month's payment application. That's the right channel for cash."

The lines never to say

Never say "we'll sort it out" or "I'm sure we can find something", because that is how a waiver is argued later. Never say "the time bar kills it" in the room either: it shuts down a conversation that may reveal facts you need, and it hardens positions before your counsel has read the notices. Never agree a number, even provisionally, without the documents. Never accept the escalation claim to buy goodwill; it is a contractor risk under your contract, and paying it sets a precedent for every remaining package. And never respond to the slow-down threat with a counter-threat.

When to stay silent

Let him finish each claim without interrupting. A contractor who feels heard is more likely to give you the facts you need, including the ones that weaken his claim. After you have said that the late claims will receive a written reservation, stop. If he pushes, say once, "That protects both of us while we look at the facts", then wait.

Holding your state

The slow-down threat is designed to raise your heart rate. Notice it, slow your breathing quietly, and lower your voice slightly. Write while he talks; note-taking gives your hands something to do and shows you are taking him seriously. If you feel the urge to defend your architect or attack his programme, ask a factual question instead: "When did your team first see the approval delay affecting the critical path?" That question matters to the notice period, and it keeps you analysing rather than reacting.

A worked example of the follow-up

Within two working days, you send one letter, reviewed by counsel, that treats each claim separately. The ground claim: notice acknowledged as received in time; assessment underway; response by a stated date. The design-change claim and the delay claim: receipt acknowledged; notices appear to fall outside the contractual period; all rights reserved, including under the notice clause; you are nevertheless willing to review the supporting facts on a without-prejudice basis. The escalation claim: the contract allocates escalation to the contractor; the claim is rejected, with the clause cited. You attach the date of the next claims review meeting. Each sentence keeps the conversation open and your position intact.

Then, internally, ask the harder question. If your architect really did approve drawings late, the prevention principle from Day 4 may weaken any time bar on the delay claim. Find out the facts from your own side before you rely on the bar. A strong position built on a weak fact is not a strong position.

What the contractor reports back to his office

Picture his email to his own director that evening. If the meeting went well from both sides, it says something like: "Owner heard all four, separated them, gave a written response date. Ground claim accepted as notified on time and under assessment. Two late ones: owner reserving rights but willing to look at our facts, so we need to get our site diaries and approval dates together. Escalation rejected under the contract, as expected. Payment application to include outstanding valued work." That email tells his director to gather evidence rather than to escalate, and it keeps your project off his list of disputes.

If the meeting went badly, the email says: "Owner refused to discuss the late claims and threatened liquidated damages", or, just as damaging to you, "Owner said they would sort something out on all four." The first pushes him toward a formal dispute. The second gives him a letter-writing campaign built on your own words. Every line in today's script is chosen so that the email he writes is the first one, not either of the others.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a friendly, informal conversation that a court later reads as accepting late claims. The control is a written reservation of rights after every meeting where late claims are discussed, and a minute recording that the discussion was without prejudice.

The beginner's mistake

Treating all the claims as one negotiation. They sit in different places under the contract, and bundling them lets the weak ones ride on the strong.

Callback

In Week 6 Kema taught acknowledge, bridge, answer for hostile questions, and "I'll confirm by Friday". Today's script is that pattern under contract: acknowledge the pressure, bridge to the process, answer in writing by a stated date.

Recap

Listen fully, separate the claims, name the process and the date, and reserve your rights in writing on anything late. Never promise, never threaten, never agree a number in the room. Check your own side's facts before relying on a time bar.

Next: Kema, Chief of staff and learning coach, on Quiz and Recap for contract forms.
checklist: I let the contractor finish each claim before responding.
I separate claims and deal with each under its own clause.
I give a date for a written response in the meeting itself.
I reserve my rights in writing on every late-notified claim.
I never agree a number in the room without the documents.
I route genuine cash pressure through the payment application.
I check my own side's facts before relying on any time bar.
The minute records that late-claim discussions were without prejudice.
head: Field checklist
speak: When a contractor brings a stack of late claims, keep the work moving and protect your rights at the same time. Thank him and acknowledge the pressure. Separate the claims, because each sits in a different place under the contract. Say you will review notice, facts and clause for each, and give a date for a written response. On the late ones, say plainly that your letter will reserve your rights, which does not stop you looking at the facts. Route real cash pressure through the payment application. Never say we'll sort it out, never say the time bar kills it, never agree a number in the room, never pay a claim the contract puts on him to buy goodwill, and never answer a slow-down threat with one of your own. Then send one counsel-reviewed letter that treats each claim separately. And before relying on a time bar, check whether your own side caused the delay.
terms: Without prejudice — a basis for settlement discussions intended to prevent what is said from being used later as an admission.
Escalation — an increase in the cost of labour or materials over time, which the contract allocates to one party.
Claims review meeting — a regular meeting to track open notices and claims, their status and next steps.

hostile.q: You keep reserving your rights. Are you going to pay any of this or not?
hostile.a: We will pay what the contract and the facts support, and we will tell you in writing by the date I gave you. The ground claim was notified on time and we are assessing it now. On the late ones, reserving our rights simply means we are not giving anything up while we review your facts, and we have said we will review them. The escalation claim sits with you under the contract, so we will not pay it. If you have facts on any claim we have not seen yet, send them this week and they will be part of our review.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Contract Forms: Six Questions on Precedence, Notices and Time Bars
summary: Six questions test the week: the three contract families, order of precedence, conditions precedent, the Hyatt Regency case, the doctrines that soften a time bar, and how to count a deadline. A Red Pen drill on a flawed notice letter and a two-minute boardroom drill close the week.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: the standard form allocates risk, but four small mechanisms, precedence, notices, conditions precedent and time bars, decide who actually pays, so read them, administer them strictly and never waive them by accident.

Recall

Q. In the late-claims meeting, what should you never say about a late claim in the room?

A. Neither "we'll sort it out", which can be argued as a waiver, nor "the time bar kills it", which shuts down the facts and hardens positions. Reserve your rights in writing instead.

Q. What is the price of a handshake term?

A. The gap between the two partners' versions applied to the distribution, plus the cost of any dispute about it.

Q. What is a tag-along right?

A. A minority partner's right to sell on the same terms when a majority partner sells.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is the first week of Phase 9, and contract administration is a skill you will use every week of every project. Answer each question aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. What are the three standard contract families, and how do you choose between them?

Answer: AIA, from the American Institute of Architects; ConsensusDocs, from a coalition of American industry associations; and FIDIC, from the International Federation of Consulting Engineers, with the Red Book for employer design, the Yellow Book for design-build and the Silver Book for turnkey work. You choose the family that matches your delivery method and location, then amend it once with a counsel-reviewed set of supplementary conditions.

Question 2. What does an order of precedence clause do, and why is coordination still needed?

Answer: It ranks the documents so the higher one governs when two conflict. But it only decides who pays for a conflict; it does not remove it. A coordination review before tender finds conflicts while fixing them is cheap.

Question 3. What is the difference between a notice obligation and a condition precedent?

Answer: A notice obligation is a duty; breaching it may cost damages. A condition precedent bars the right unless notice is given, and courts usually need clear words, such as "shall not be entitled unless", to read a clause that way. Verify against the governing law.

Question 4. What was the root cause of the Hyatt Regency walkway collapse, and what is Rule 77?

Answer: A change from continuous to split hanger rods doubled the load on the fourth-floor connection and moved through shop drawing review without being checked as a design change; the original connection had also not been proved to code. Rule 77: no design change reaches the field through a shop drawing, submittal or email unless it is flagged as a change and the designer of record accepts it in writing, with the calculation for anything structural or life-safety.

Question 5. Name three doctrines that can soften a time bar.

Answer: Waiver and estoppel, when a party acts as though a late notice were valid; the prevention principle, when the party relying on the bar caused the delay without an extension mechanism; and good faith or honest-performance duties in some systems. Each varies by jurisdiction.

Question 6. What three things must you find in a clause before counting a notice deadline?

Answer: What starts the clock, whether the period runs in calendar or working days, and the deemed receipt rule for the method used. Then count from Day 0, check holidays, and set an internal deadline a week earlier.

Recap of the week

Day 1 introduced the three families and the four mechanisms. Day 2 took the Hyatt Regency through seven steps and produced Rule 77. Day 3 priced a time bar, a bid premium and a coordination review. Day 4 set out how courts treat notices and conditions, what softens a time bar, and how Canada and Guyana compare. Day 5 counted three deadlines and priced a missed one. Day 6 scripted the late-claims meeting.

Red Pen

Read this hypothetical owner's reply to a late claim and find the defects before reading on.

"Hi Dave, thanks for the delay claim. Honestly it's a bit late but I'm sure we can find a fair number between us. Let's talk Thursday and sort it out. Also, re the steel price rise, we'll see what we can do. Sent to dave@contractor's personal email. Cheers."

Say that out loud now.

The defects. First, no reservation of rights: "a bit late but I'm sure we can find a fair number" invites an argument that you waived the time bar. Second, "sort it out" signals a commitment to settle before the facts are reviewed. Third, the letter does not cite the clause or state that the notice falls outside the contractual period. Fourth, it is sent to a personal email rather than the address named in the notice clause, so it may not count as a valid notice at all. Fifth, it softens on the steel claim, which the contract allocates to the contractor, creating a precedent for every remaining package. Sixth, it gives no date for a formal written response and no basis for the Thursday discussion, such as without prejudice. A corrected letter acknowledges receipt, cites the clause, states the notice appears late, reserves all rights, offers a without-prejudice review of the facts, rejects the escalation claim with the clause, and goes to the contractual address.

One more habit from this drill. Before you send any letter about a claim, read it once as the contractor's lawyer would, looking for a sentence that sounds like agreement, and once as a judge would, looking for whether it reached the right person by the right method. If either reader would find something, rewrite it before it leaves.

The boardroom drill

Set a two-minute timer. Explain to an imagined lender's credit committee how you manage the construction contract. Then compare with this model answer.

"We use a standard form matched to our delivery method, amended by a set of supplementary conditions our counsel reviewed once and reuses. Before tender, our designers run a coordination review so the order of precedence is a safety net, not a weapon. Notices are formal: named recipients, a shared project address, proof of delivery. Our project manager keeps a register of every notice with its trigger, clause, type of day, receipt rule and deadline, checked by a second person, and every site meeting ends by asking whether anything needs a notice. Any late claim gets a written reservation of rights before we discuss its facts. Submittals must declare deviations, and structural changes need the engineer's written acceptance with a calculation. And we priced our amendments both ways, the claims they prevent and the premium they add to bids."

Score yourself. Did you open with the bottom line? Did you mention precedence, notices, time bars and change control? Did you finish inside two minutes? If not, record it again tomorrow.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is learning the mechanisms and then letting a friendly site culture undo them, one informal email at a time. The control is the register and the reservation habit, applied to every contractor, however good the relationship.

The beginner's mistake

Thinking that the lawyer handles notices. The lawyer drafts the clause. Your project team either follows it or loses its protection.

Callback

In Week 48 Marco taught the owner decision log. A notices register is its contractual twin: the decision log records what you decided, and the register records what the contract required you to say, and when.

Recap

Choose the form to fit the delivery method. Read precedence, notices, conditions precedent and time bars. Coordinate before tender, count deadlines properly, route every change through the designer, and reserve your rights in writing.

Next: LEX, Contracts and law, on First Principles: risk allocation through indemnities, limitation of liability and consequential loss.

head: The six questions
speak: This week was about the standard construction contract and the four mechanisms that decide who pays. The AIA, ConsensusDocs and FIDIC families pre-allocate risk; choose the one that matches your delivery method and amend it once with counsel. The order of precedence decides which document wins a conflict, but a coordination review before tender is what removes the conflict. A notice obligation is a duty; a condition precedent bars the right unless notice is given, and needs clear words. A time bar is a condition precedent with a clock, softened in some systems by waiver, estoppel, the prevention principle and good faith duties, so always reserve your rights in writing before discussing a late claim. The Hyatt Regency collapse gave Rule 77: route every design change through the designer of record in writing. Count deadlines from the clause, not from memory, and keep a notices register.
terms: Supplementary conditions — an owner's standard amendments applied to a chosen contract form.
Notices register — a log of every contractual notice sent and received, with clause, dates and deadlines.
Red Pen — a drill in which you read a short document looking for planted defects before they are revealed.

hostile.q: Your contractor says your team agreed in a meeting to pay a late claim. Did you?
hostile.a: I would check the minute first, and I expect it to show that our team listened, separated the claims and said a written response would follow. Our practice is that no commitment on any claim is made in a meeting, and that every late claim receives a written reservation of rights. If the minute or any email from our side says otherwise, I want to know, and I will take advice on it. But a conversation in a site meeting is not, on its own, a notice or an agreement under this contract.
